chapters.caption: The National Gallery from Trafalgar Square — free, and full of masterpieces
chapters.directions: Enter via the Sainsbury Wing entrance (the main entrance since its 2025 reopening, at the Trafalgar Square corner) and head up to the main gallery floor.
chapters.text: Here's the astonishing thing about this building: everything in it is free, and almost everything in it is a masterpiece. The National Gallery holds the national collection of Western European painting from about 1250 to 1900 — over 2,300 paintings, more than 1,000 of them on display — and it belongs, quite literally, to the British public. It began in 1824 when the government bought 38 paintings from a banker's collection and decided, unusually for the time, that the nation's art should be kept in the centre of London where working people could actually see it, rather than in a royal palace out of town. That democratic idea still shapes the place: no ticket, no turnstile, just walk in off Trafalgar Square. Our route follows the building's own logic — roughly chronological, from gold-ground medieval altarpieces in the Sainsbury Wing, through the Renaissance, to Turner, Constable, and the Impressionists. A word of strategy: this gallery rewards choosing. We'll hit the essential paintings — the ones you'd kick yourself for missing — and move at a pace that lets you actually look. Paintings are sometimes lent or moved between rooms, so if a favourite isn't where you expect, ask a gallery assistant; they know where everything is hiding. Ready? Let's start with paintings older than the printing press.
chapters.title: Welcome — A Free Gallery of Masterpieces

chapters.caption: Early Renaissance rooms in the Sainsbury Wing — gold grounds and the birth of perspective
chapters.directions: Stay in the Sainsbury Wing and continue through the early Renaissance rooms toward Botticelli and Leonardo.
chapters.text: Start in the Sainsbury Wing, where the oldest paintings live, and give your eyes a moment to adjust to the gold. These medieval and early Renaissance panels were made as altarpieces — working religious objects, glowing by candlelight — and their gold grounds aren't decoration so much as theology: that's the light of heaven, beaten into leaf. Look for Paolo Uccello's Battle of San Romano, a huge, strange, wonderful panel of a Florentine battle rendered as a pageant — lances laid out like pick-up sticks to show off the new science of perspective, which Uccello was so obsessed with that his wife complained he stayed up all night murmuring about vanishing points. Then find the painting everyone comes to this wing for: Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait, from 1434, one of the most analysed pictures on Earth. A merchant and his wife stand in a Bruges bedroom, every surface — brass chandelier, oranges, little dog, discarded clogs — painted with jewel-like precision. Now get close and find the convex mirror on the back wall: it reflects the entire room, including two extra figures in the doorway, one of whom may be van Eyck himself. Above the mirror, in elaborate Latin script, he signed it not 'Jan van Eyck made this' but 'Jan van Eyck was here.' A witness statement, in paint. Take your time — this small picture repays every second.
chapters.title: Early Renaissance — Uccello and the Arnolfini Portrait

chapters.caption: Botticelli's Venus and Mars (c. 1485) — love conquers war, with wasps
chapters.directions: Continue through the Sainsbury Wing toward the Leonardo room (the Virgin of the Rocks).
chapters.text: Now find Sandro Botticelli's Venus and Mars, painted around 1485, and enjoy one of the slyest pictures of the Renaissance. The subject sounds grand — the goddess of love and the god of war — but Botticelli plays it as gentle comedy. Mars, the great warrior, is fast asleep, utterly knocked out after lovemaking, while little satyrs play with his armour: one blows a conch shell in his ear (he doesn't stir), another hauls away his lance, a third has crawled inside his breastplate. Venus, by contrast, sits wide awake, serene and completely in charge. The message, for the Florentine household this was probably painted for — likely a wedding picture — is clear and cheering: love conquers war. Now look for the detail most visitors miss, down in the bottom right corner: wasps are nesting in the hollow of a tree trunk by Mars's head. Wasps — vespe in Italian — were the emblem of the Vespucci family, a delicious visual pun for the probable patrons, and perhaps a little warning that love has a sting. Botticelli's line is the thing to savour throughout: that flowing, calligraphic contour that makes everything look like it's dancing, even a snoring god. The gallery has more Botticelli nearby, including the Mystic Nativity — painted in the anxious year 1500, full of apocalyptic inscriptions — but Venus and Mars is the charmer. Let it charm you.
chapters.title: Botticelli — Venus and Mars

chapters.caption: Leonardo da Vinci, The Virgin of the Rocks (c. 1491–1508)
chapters.directions: From Leonardo, move into the High Renaissance rooms for Michelangelo and Raphael, then on toward Titian.
chapters.text: In a dim room nearby hangs one of the gallery's supreme treasures: Leonardo da Vinci's Virgin of the Rocks. The scene is an invented legend — the young John the Baptist meeting the Christ Child in the wilderness — set not in a landscape but in a shadowy grotto of wet rocks and strange flowers, lit by something between daylight and a dream. Mary reaches protectively over the infant John, who prays toward Jesus; Jesus, a toddler, raises two fingers in blessing; and an angel kneels behind, pointing — and looking straight out at you with an expression people have argued about for 500 years. Everything here is Leonardo's signature technique: sfumato, form modelled in smoke-soft transitions with almost no hard edges, so faces seem to emerge from shadow the way thoughts emerge in the mind. There are actually two versions of this composition — this one, and an earlier one in the Louvre — and scholars have spent careers on which parts Leonardo painted himself; the current scholarly view gives him more of this London version than was once thought. While you're in this room, don't miss the Burlington House Cartoon nearby: a huge, fragile charcoal drawing of the Virgin and Child with saints, the only large Leonardo drawing to survive — you are looking at his hand moving across the paper, five centuries ago. It is, for many visitors, the most quietly thrilling object in the building.
chapters.title: Leonardo — The Virgin of the Rocks

chapters.caption: High Renaissance Rome — Michelangelo's Entombment and Raphael's Madonnas
chapters.directions: Continue into the Venetian rooms for Titian.
chapters.text: The High Renaissance rooms put the two giants side by side, and the contrast is the lesson. Michelangelo's Entombment, from about 1500–01, is one of only a handful of his panel paintings — and it's unfinished, which is precisely why you should linger. Christ's body is carried by solemn figures against a landscape that stops mid-thought: areas of bare preparation, drapery resolved in one place and sketched in another. You are watching the greatest sculptor of the age think in paint, in his mid-twenties, and abandon the panel — probably because Rome, Julius II, and marble were calling. Raphael, a few years younger, is the opposite experience: everything finished, balanced, serene. His Madonnas here — look for the Ansidei Madonna and the luminous Garvagh Madonna — show why contemporaries thought he'd achieved perfection: compositions so harmonious they look inevitable, tenderness without a drop of sentimentality. Raphael died at 37, Michelangelo lived to 88 and spent decades insisting he was a sculptor, not a painter — and yet here they are, forever sharing a wall. While you're in these rooms, also seek out Hans Holbein's The Ambassadors in the Northern Renaissance displays nearby: two French envoys surrounded by the instruments of Renaissance learning, and at their feet, a smear that resolves — only when you view it from a sharp angle at the side — into a perfect skull. A memento mori hidden in plain sight. Walk to the side and watch it snap into focus; it's the gallery's best magic trick.
chapters.title: Michelangelo and Raphael — The High Renaissance

chapters.caption: Titian, Bacchus and Ariadne (1520–23) — Venetian colour at full blast
chapters.directions: Move on to the 17th-century rooms for the Dutch masters — Rembrandt and Vermeer.
chapters.text: If Leonardo is smoke, Titian is fireworks. Bacchus and Ariadne, painted in 1520–23 for the Duke of Ferrara's private study, may be the most joyful painting in the building. The story: Ariadne, abandoned on the island of Naxos by her lover Theseus (that's his ship, sailing away on the left), is startled by the arrival of Bacchus, god of wine, who leaps from his cheetah-drawn chariot — cheetahs, note, because Titian's patron kept real ones — so in love at first sight that he's frozen mid-air, drapery flying. Above Ariadne's head, the stars into which her crown will be transformed already glitter. But honestly, the story is an excuse for the colour: that sky is ultramarine made from lapis lazuli imported from Afghanistan, more expensive than gold, and Titian lays it on like he owns the mine. Look at the whole choreography of reds, whites, and blues sweeping across the canvas, the little dog barking at the satyr, the revellers hauling a calf's head — it's a painting that moves. Titian was in his thirties and announcing himself as the greatest colourist in Europe; five centuries later, standing in front of this, the claim still holds. The Venetian rooms around it — Veronese's vast Family of Darius, Tintoretto's drama — extend the lesson: in Venice, colour wasn't decoration. Colour was the argument.
chapters.title: Titian — Bacchus and Ariadne

chapters.caption: Rembrandt's self-portraits — a whole life, painted honestly
chapters.directions: Continue to the British rooms for Turner and Constable.
chapters.text: Now for the north — and a change of key, from Venetian sunshine to Dutch candlelight. The 17th-century Dutch rooms hold two of the gallery's most intimate encounters. First, Johannes Vermeer: look for his young women at the virginal — a small keyboard instrument — in quiet, light-washed interiors. There are only about 37 Vermeers in the world, and the National Gallery has two beauties. Notice how he builds a whole psychology out of geometry and daylight: a window on the left, a map on the wall, a woman pausing mid-thought. Nothing happens, and somehow everything happens. Then, Rembrandt — and here the gallery gives you something almost no other museum can: a life in self-portraits. Find the Self Portrait at the Age of 34, painted in 1640 at the height of his fame and fortune: confident, richly dressed, deliberately echoing Raphael and Titian, a man composing his own legend. Then find the Self Portrait at the Age of 63, from 1669, the year of his death — bankrupt, bereaved, his great loves and his money gone — and painted with a freedom and honesty that makes the young man's portrait look like theatre. The paint itself is sculptural, the face emerging from darkness like something carved out of experience. Same man, 29 years apart, hanging in the same collection. Stand between those two portraits for a while. It's the most human moment in the gallery.
chapters.title: Dutch Masters — Vermeer and Rembrandt

chapters.caption: Turner, The Fighting Temeraire (1839) — voted Britain's favourite painting
chapters.directions: Head to the Impressionist and Post-Impressionist rooms for the final stretch — Monet, Seurat, and Van Gogh.
chapters.text: Welcome to the British rooms, and to the painting Britain voted its favourite in a national poll: J.M.W. Turner's Fighting Temeraire, from 1839. The subject is an ending. The Temeraire was a 98-gun warship, second in line at Trafalgar in 1805, a genuine hero of the Napoleonic Wars. By 1838 she was obsolete — a rotting hulk — and Turner shows her last journey: being towed up the Thames to the breaker's yard by a small, black, smoky paddle tug. The old ship glows like a ghost in golden light, sails furled, flags still flying, while the tug — the future, steam-powered and sooty — does the actual work. Turner took liberties (the masts and rigging had already been removed, and the tow went the other way), because he wasn't painting a news report; he was painting the passing of the age of sail, and of his own age too — he was 64. Everything Turner knew about light is in that sky. Nearby, look for Rain, Steam, and Speed, where a train hurtles over a bridge through a shimmering downpour — Turner embracing the very modernity that killed the Temeraire, and finding it just as sublime. And find the little hare, bottom right of the train picture, running for its life: old nature, outrunning — just barely — the machine. Turner bequeathed his work to the nation, which is why this gallery's Turner holdings are so rich. He wanted to be here, free, for everyone. He is.
chapters.title: Turner — The Fighting Temeraire

chapters.caption: Constable, The Hay Wain (1821) — England's most famous landscape
chapters.directions: Continue into the final rooms — the Impressionists and Post-Impressionists.
chapters.text: In the same British rooms, find John Constable's Hay Wain — possibly the most famous landscape England ever produced, and a painting with a deliciously ironic history. Constable painted it in 1821: a horse-drawn hay cart fording the River Stour in Suffolk, beside Flatford Mill, with a dog, a boatman, and a sky that takes up half the canvas and does most of the talking. Constable was revolutionary about skies — he called them 'the chief organ of sentiment' in a landscape, studied clouds like a meteorologist, and made annotated sky sketches that scientists still admire. He painted the Suffolk countryside he grew up in, at full scale, outdoors-informed, with a freshness nobody in London wanted: the Hay Wain failed to sell in England. Then it was shown in Paris in 1824 — and the French went wild. It won a gold medal from the French king, influenced a generation of French painters, and Constable came home a prophet honoured everywhere except, commercially, at home. Stand back for the whole effect, then go close and look at the white highlights — flicked on with a palette knife, contemporaries called it 'Constable's snow' — sparkling on the water and foliage. The scene still exists, by the way: Willy Lott's house, on the left, still stands at Flatford, and the view is barely changed. Constable's great rival Turner is in the same rooms; the two men defined British landscape in opposite ways — Turner dissolving the world into light, Constable grounding it in one loved valley. You get to judge the contest, free, any day of the week.
chapters.title: Constable — The Hay Wain

chapters.caption: Van Gogh, Sunflowers (1888) — one of five versions, painted for Gauguin
chapters.directions: From the Impressionist rooms, loop back toward the central hall — the free galleries mean you can return any time for a second look.
chapters.text: The final rooms bring the story into modernity, and the crowds will tell you where the star is before you see it: Vincent van Gogh's Sunflowers, painted in Arles in 1888. Van Gogh made a series of sunflower still lifes to decorate the little yellow house he'd rented in the south of France, hoping Paul Gauguin would join him and they'd found an artists' colony. This version — fifteen flowers in a simple vase against a blazing yellow ground — is the fourth version, and it's become one of the most beloved paintings in the world. Look closely at the paint handling: every petal and seed head is built from distinct, directional strokes, so the flowers seem to twist and radiate; and notice the audacity of the colour scheme — yellow on yellow on yellow, a symphony in one note that somehow never gets monotonous. Around it, the Impressionist rooms give the context: Monet's Water-Lily Pond, with its green Japanese bridge at Giverny, all shimmer and reflection; Claude Monet's Thames paintings too, London fog turned to lavender and gold. And don't miss Georges Seurat's Bathers at Asnières, painted when he was 24 — a huge, calm scene of Parisians by the river, built (look closely) from the beginnings of his pointillist technique, tiny distinct touches of colour that fuse in your eye. In 1884 the establishment rejected it. Now schoolchildren are brought to see it as a foundation stone of modern art. There's a lesson in that, and this gallery — free, national, patient — is full of it.
chapters.title: Impressionists and Van Gogh — Sunflowers

chapters.caption: Trafalgar Square from the gallery steps — come back any time, it's free
chapters.directions: Exit to Trafalgar Square. Charing Cross and Leicester Square stations are both a few minutes' walk.
chapters.text: As you head back down toward Trafalgar Square, here's my closing advice — and it's the best thing about this entire gallery: you can come back. Today we did the essential National Gallery: van Eyck's mirror, Leonardo's grotto, Botticelli's wasps, Titian's ultramarine, Rembrandt's two ages of man, Turner's ghost ship, Constable's river, and Van Gogh's sunflowers. That's a highlights route of roughly two hours — but the collection holds over a thousand more paintings on display, including Velázquez's Rokeby Venus (the only female nude by the greatest Spanish painter, slashed by a suffragette in 1914 and lovingly restored), Holbein's Ambassadors with its hidden skull, Caravaggio's swaggering late works, and whole rooms of French and British art we walked past. Because admission is free, the smart way to use this place is the way Londoners do: in small doses, one wing at a time, twenty minutes with one great painting rather than a footsore march past two hundred. If you have a Friday, come in the evening — the gallery stays open late, the crowds thin, and the Arnolfini Portrait by lamplight, in a quiet room, is a different and better painting than the one surrounded by tour groups at noon. Thanks for walking with me. The nation's paintings will be here, free, whenever you're ready for more.
chapters.title: Wrap-Up — The Route, and Coming Back

intro: This is the nation's painting collection — Western European art from the 1200s to 1900, over a thousand paintings on display, in a grand building on Trafalgar Square — and it is completely free. Our route is the essential one: we start in the Sainsbury Wing with medieval gold and the Arnolfini Portrait, walk through Botticelli, Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael and Titian, meet Rembrandt and Vermeer, then finish with Britain's own Turner and Constable before the Impressionists and Van Gogh's Sunflowers. About two hours at a looking pace. Because it's free, treat this as a first visit, not a once-ever visit — the Londoner's way is little and often.
mapNote: The gallery is arranged in four wings around a central hall, and the collection runs roughly chronologically. The Sainsbury Wing (west side, now the main entrance) holds the earliest art, 1200s–1500: Uccello, van Eyck, Botticelli, Leonardo. The West Wing continues 1500–1600 (Michelangelo, Raphael, Titian, Holbein). The North Wing covers 1600–1700 (Dutch masters, Rembrandt, Vermeer, Caravaggio, Velázquez). The East Wing runs 1700–1900: Turner, Constable, then the Impressionists and Post-Impressionists (Monet, Seurat, Van Gogh) in the furthest rooms. Room numbers change as displays rotate — use the free gallery plan, and check the gallery's website or ask staff for a specific painting's current room.
practical: Admission to the permanent collection is free, every day. A free timed entry ticket booked online can speed entry at busy times, but walk-up entry is also available.
Enter via the Sainsbury Wing entrance on Trafalgar Square — since the wing's reopening it's the main entrance, with step-free access.
Friday evenings (open until 21:00) are the connoisseur's slot: the Impressionist rooms and the Arnolfini Portrait are far quieter after 19:00.
Paintings move: loans and rehangs mean a specific picture's room can change. Check the gallery website's painting pages (each lists its current room) before you cross the building for one picture.
Large bags and wheeled luggage aren't allowed in the galleries; there's a cloakroom on the ground floor.
Do it in doses. Because it's free, one wing per visit beats a marathon — and the gallery's free daily guided tours and talks are an excellent way to go deeper.

Photography without flash is allowed in most permanent galleries — but the best souvenir here is time spent looking; give the Arnolfini mirror and the Rembrandt self-portraits a full five minutes each.
subtitle: Free masterpieces on Trafalgar Square — from van Eyck to Van Gogh
title: National Gallery
